questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests understanding of basic CI gates for Kubernetes manifests and how to enforce namespace discipline across a multi-service repository. It demonstrates practical knowledge of YAML parsing, GitHub Actions, and Kubernetes resource management.

## Key Concepts

- **YAML manifest parsing with yq**: Using yq to extract and validate metadata.namespace fields across all Kubernetes manifests
- **Namespace discipline**: Enforcing non-default namespaces prevents accidental deployments to unintended environments and ensures proper resource isolation
- **Lightweight CI gates**: Simple, fast validation scripts every PR without that run on requiring external tools or complex infrastructure
- **Cluster-scoped vs namespace-scoped resources**: Understanding when to omit namespace (ClusterRole, CRDs) versus when it must be present (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap)

## What Separates Good Answers from Great Ones

A great answer recognizes that not all Kubernetes resources are namespace-scoped. Cluster-scoped resources like ClusterRole, ClusterRoleBinding, CustomResourceDefinition, and Nodes must be excluded from this validation. The candidate should handle this edge case gracefully, either by skipping these resource types or by documenting the assumption that only namespace-scoped resources are being validated.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests foundational secure supply chain practices in a beginner-friendly manner. It mirrors real-world CI gates used in production environments around Dockerfile hygiene, image signing, SBOM generation, and registry controls. It introduces modern tools like Cosign and SBOM attestations without overwhelming complexity.

## Key Concepts

- **Dockerfile Hygiene**: Non-root USER and multi-stage builds reduce security vulnerabilities and image size
- **Container Image Signing**: Using Cosign to sign and verify container images ensures integrity
- **SBOM Attestation**: Software Bill of Materials provides transparency into image contents and dependencies
- **GitHub Actions Workflows**: Implementing gates and policy checks in CI/CD pipelines
- **Registry Allowlist**: Restricting deployments to approved registries prevents supply chain attacks

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal GitHub Actions workflow
name: Docker Security Gate
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Validate Dockerfile
        run: |
          # Check for non-root USER
          grep -q 'USER ' Dockerfile || exit 1
          # Check for multi-stage build
          grep -q 'FROM.*AS' Dockerfile || exit 1
      
      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build -t ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: |
          syft ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }} -o spdx-json > sbom.json
      
      - name: Sign image and SBOM with Cosign
        run: |
          cosign sign ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
          cosign attest --type spdx-json --predicate sbom.json ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Verify signature and attestation
        run: |
          cosign verify ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design a scalable, automated policy gate across multi-cloud clusters using Gatekeeper/OPA, Cosign attestations, and runtime security constraints.

## Key Concepts

- Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
- Cosign attestation and image provenance
- Registry allowlist and image provenance checks
- Pod security: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, drop capabilities
- CI integration and gatekeeper audit verification

## Code Example

```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (Gatekeeper) minimal sketch
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8ssecuredcontainers
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sSecuredContainers
  targets:
    - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
      rego: |
        package k8ssecuredcontainers
        
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
          not signed(container.image)
          msg := sprintf("Container image %v must be cosign-signed", [container.image])
        }
        
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
          not allowed_registry(container.image)
          msg := sprintf("Registry %v not in allowlist", [container.image])
        }
        
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
          not container.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
          msg := "Container must run as non-root"
        }
```

## What to Look For

- Demonstrates understanding of OPA/Gatekeeper policy structure
- Shows proper cosign attestation validation approach
- Includes comprehensive runtime security constraints
- Outlines practical CI/CD integration strategy

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to enforce secure secret handling across multi-cloud clusters, using policy-as-code, and integrating cert-manager with GitOps pipelines.

## Key Concepts
- Policy as code (Kyverno/OPA)
- cert-manager Certificate -> Secret flow
- ExternalSecret / SecretStore integration
- CI gating and canary verification

## Code Example
```yaml
# Kyverno policy (example)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-inline-tls-and-enforce-secretref
spec:
  validationFailureAction: fail
  rules:
  - name: deny-inline-tls
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Deployment", "StatefulSet"]
    validate:
      message: "TLS data must come from cert-manager SecretRef; do not inline certificates"
      pattern:
        spec:
          template:
            spec:
              volumes:
              - secret:
                  secretName: "?!*"
```

```rego
# OPA/ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (illustrative)
package kubernetes.admission

deny[{"msg":"inline certs not allowed"}] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Deployment" or input.request.kind.kind == "StatefulSet"
  some i
  secret := input.request.object.spec.template.spec.volumes[i]
  secret.secretName != "" # ensure SecretRef used, not inline data
}
```

```yaml
# Failing manifest (inline cert example)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: tls-secret
type: kubernetes.io/tls
data:
  tls.crt: LS0tLS1CRUdJTiBDRVJUSUZJQ0FURS0tLS0t... # inline cert data
  tls.key: LS0tLS1CRUdJTiBSU0EgUFJ...
```

```yaml
# Passing manifest (SecretRef to cert-manager Secret)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      volumes:
      - name: tls
        secret:
          secretName: my-cert-manager-secret
```

```yaml
# CI validation steps (high level)
- lint manifests
- run policy gate (Kyverno/OPA) on PR
- validate that Deployment references cert-manager Secret (no inline data)
- run a quick canary test in a staging cluster
```

- How would you test this in a mono-repo with many teams?

## Why This Question Is Asked

This question evaluates the ability to design admission-time policy enforcement for sensitive data in multi-tenant environments. It tests understanding of tying secret handling to external stores, per-tenant encryption keys, and namespace-level controls—all critical for regulated workloads in cloud-native platforms.

## Key Concepts

- **Policy as Code (OPA/Rego)**: Declarative policies evaluated at admission control time, enabling infrastructure teams to enforce security and compliance requirements programmatically.

- **Secrets Management**: SecretStore/CSI driver integration allows secrets to be sourced from external stores with envelope encryption using tenant-managed KMS keys, ensuring cryptographic isolation between tenants.

- **Multi-Tenancy**: Namespace-level labeling combined with EncryptionPolicy CRDs provides a declarative mechanism to enforce tenant boundaries and encryption requirements across all namespaced resources.

- **Admission Control**: Gatekeeper policies act as validation webhooks that intercept resource creation and modification requests, blocking non-compliant resources before they enter the cluster.
